A new botanical-conservation photographic concept shows a woman with the attached face and hair guidance carefully moving a seedling tray to safety. The supplied photograph guides the visible face and hair: a dark chin-length bob with fine separated bangs, large dark brown eyes, a softly tapered face, a straight nose and softly full pink lips. She is at a botanical field station after a tidal surge. A dark water mark crosses the plaster below the workbench, damp silt remains on the lower floor, and two rescued trays already occupy a dry shelf. Her last shallow tray holds upright salt-tolerant seedlings, droplets still bright on their leaves. At the shutter, the tray has just reached the raised shelf at her right; both hands steady its separated front corners, fingers visibly meeting the rim. Her shoulders, bent elbows and wrists form connected arm paths beside her torso. The supporting shelf carries the tray's weight, and her feet stand squarely on a stable wooden grate. Her torso turns slightly toward the tray while her face lifts toward the dry shelf, concentration softening into a small exhale as she sees the plants secure. She wears a warm ivory linen wrap blouse with overlapping diagonal front panels and a matching waist sash tied into one visible bow at her front waist, two loops and two loose ends resting against the blouse, over olive straight trousers. The working hands and tray sit to the side of her waist so the garment front remains readable. The cloth creases at her elbows and waist belong to the exertion of this moment. Frame her from head to just below her boots, close enough that her face, the waist tie and both hand contacts are distinct, with the wet floor and dry shelf held in the same portrait composition. Cool dawn enters the tall window behind the shelf while a warm task lamp brings gentle life to her face and the linen texture. Natural photographic perspective, clear edge separation and restrained color make the precarious recovery feel inhabited, intimate and practical.
